Trend picks

Trend picks come from the situation rather than the model: record, scoring margin, recent form, home/road splits, rest, overtime the night before, streaks and bad losses. Each factor shows how often teams in that spot won in past games; factors that never held up are listed but not counted. A side needs at least 3 live factors and a clear edge over the opponent's. The ladder compares every way to bet the side against the model's fair price, and the grade says whether the price leaves anything on the table. Trends are often already in the price, so many trend picks grade C or D. They're tracked as their own category so the record shows whether they beat the model.

How it works

Data. Box scores for this season and last come from ESPN via the sportsdataverse data releases on GitHub, topped up with ESPN game summaries for anything newer. Schedules, sportsbook lines (ESPN's odds feed, usually DraftKings), the league injury report and team rosters come from ESPN's public API. Player prop prices are read from ESPN's prop feed when it has them.

Team ratings. Each team gets an offensive, defensive and pace rating per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent, home court and back-to-backs, from a weighted regression where a game from 20 days ago counts half as much as last night. Last season's ratings seed the new season, pulled 45% toward average and adjusted for roster changes (players gained and lost, valued by game score per 36 minutes). That seed is worth about 5 games, so by mid-November this season dominates.

Injuries. Each player's value is his game score per 36 minutes over a replacement player, times his minutes. If he's out, the team loses that value, minus whatever the ratings already reflect from games he has missed. Questionable counts as 50% to play, doubtful 20%, day-to-day 70%.

Game estimate. Pace times efficiency gives each team's points. For betting, the model is blended with the market when a line is posted: 35% model on the spread and moneyline, 20% on totals. Results land within about 13.6 points of the spread estimate and 18.7 of the total estimate (one standard deviation), which sets every probability.

Why blend? Tested on 554 games of 2025-26 with closing lines, the model alone missed the final margin by 13.6 points on average (root mean square) against 13.5 for the closing line, and the 35/65 blend beat both at 13.4. On totals the closing line was clearly better (18.7 vs 19.2), so the model only nudges totals. When the model disagreed with the closing spread by 3+ points, its side covered 54.8% (109-90), but that test knew who actually played. Treat any single edge as thin.

Players. Minutes come from recent games for the current team (coach's-decision DNPs count as zero), blended with last season, then injured teammates' minutes are spread across the rotation, capped at 40. Per-minute rates weight recent games most, scaled so the team's players add up to its projected points, with pace and the opponent's rebounding and assists allowed. Each stat's spread comes from the player's own game log, widened to match how often projections hit in a 2025-26 backtest, where they beat a last-10-games average on points, rebounds, assists and PRA.

Odds. Fair is the break-even price for our probability. Bet at subtracts a safety margin (2.5 points for main markets, 3.5 for team totals and halves, 4.0 for props). At Bet at or better is value, between Bet at and Fair is a lean, worse than Fair is a pass.

Top bets. Only markets with a real sportsbook price qualify. A pick is either high probability (our 58%+ and the price beats fair) or value (the price beats Bet at). The list alternates between the two, takes at most 2 per game and never both sides of one market, and skips bets where the model and market disagree by more than 17 points, which usually means news the model can't see.

Limits. Late scratches, rest days announced at shootaround and trades after the run aren't known. Run it again close to tip-off and check the injury report. I'm not a financial advisor; bet only what you can afford to lose.

Grades, trends and units

Grades. Every pick gets a score out of 100: edge at the price (30), win chance (10), how close the model is to the market (10; a huge gap usually means news the model can't see), whether situational trends back the side (30) and how much the model's claimed edge has held up in that bet type (20). A is 68+, B 56+, C 44+, D below. Unpriced picks and early-season picks top out at B. Hover a grade for the breakdown.

Trend picks. Each side is checked for situational factors: a better record, scoring margin or recent form, a home/road split, the opponent on a back-to-back or coming off overtime, rest, streaks and the opponent's last loss being to a worse team. Each factor's record comes from past games, and only factors that won more than half the time (after mixing in 60 games of 50/50) count. A trend pick needs 3+ of them and a net edge over the opponent's factors. The "ways to bet it" ladder compares the moneyline, regulation or spread and team total against the model's fair price, and the play is the one with the best expected return.

Suggested units. 0.25 Kelly (1 unit = 1% of a bankroll), rounded to half units and capped at 3u. Before sizing, the model's win chance is pulled toward the market by the bet type's trust: trust = the share of the model's claimed edge that has actually shown up in graded results, starting at 50% and updating as games finish. A bet type that has matched the market and not the model gets small or zero units.

Scatter. On the Track record tab every priced pick is placed by its edge at the price (across) and the price (up), coloured by result, with upcoming picks as rings. Zones shade areas where at least 5 graded picks made or lost money, so you can see whether tonight's picks sit where past ones paid.
